job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Priya Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I graduated in June with an accounting and finance degree from Northfield University. Most days I wake up in the box room at my parents' flat in Hadley, send three or four applications before lunch, then help my little brother with his maths. My mum works nights as a nurse, so the flat is quiet until she gets in at eight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest part is the silence after you apply. I've sent about sixty applications and got maybe six replies, most of them automatic rejections. What I still like is the actual work: during my eight-week internship at Pell and Cray, a small audit firm, I did bank reconciliations and I loved how a messy page finally balanced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it means nothing scary happens. But at the same time, nothing gets better for people like me either. At home I'd tell my mum that it's the same old slow market, and online I'd probably stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be stuck. I have about 14,000 in student loans and roughly six weeks of money saved. If AI is only hype, the firms still keep their graduate intake small and call it cost control, and that's not fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, ten a week, and ask Mr Pell at my old internship if he knows anyone hiring. I'd also take shifts at the garden centre on Marsh Road so I'm not asking my mum for money. I wouldn't try any AI tools, because I don't trust them with my numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels flat and tiring. I'm not scared of a robot, I'm scared of a rent-free room running out of patience, even though my parents never say a word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned sixty applications. What happens to them on the employer's side, as far as you can tell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly sure the software already filters us. I got a rejection email four minutes after I applied once, so nobody read it. The routine tasks I trained on, like matching invoices, are the ones that quietly go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or choice gets squeezed first if the search drags on another six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The garden centre hours would go up and my savings would stop growing. I'd stop buying train tickets to interviews unless it's a real shortlist, and my brother's birthday present would be small this year.

say: I'd tell friends **nothing much changes**, which is fine, but graduates still get a bad deal.
I'd keep **quiet online**, because complaining about applications doesn't get anyone hired.
think: I'm stuck on the **same ladder** with 14,000 of loans, and hype or not, the firms keep graduate intakes small.
I worry the **automatic filters** already decide my fate before anyone reads my name.
do: Send **ten applications a week** and ask my old internship boss for contacts.
Take **extra garden centre shifts** so I don't lean on my mum for money.
Skip AI tools and **cut interview train trips** to real shortlists only.
feel: I feel **flat and tired**, mostly guilty about still living in the box room.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of a robot, I'm scared of a rent-free room running out of patience, even though my parents never say a word.
fieldNote: Priya is **already worried** before any AI change; debt, no offer and no income decide her mood.
She blames firms that keep graduate intakes small, not the technology, which fits her left-leaning view.
Her refusal to try AI tools shows in every plan: no learning, only more of the same effort.

steps.text: Send ten job applications every week
Pick up extra shifts at the Marsh Road garden centre
Skip interview train trips unless a real shortlist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is where the unions and the government should step in. If firms use software to cut graduate hiring, there should be rules about it and public help for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm exactly in the firing line. Reconciliations, checking invoices and filling in tax forms are what an entry-level accountant does, and those are the thinking tasks on that card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to public bodies, the council and the health service finance team, where there's a union and an actual rulebook. I'd ask my mum's friend at the hospital about the finance office. I'd probably sign up for the graduate union branch, and maybe do one free online course on how software does audits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unfair and a bit angry. I studied for three years to be the person who checks things, and now the checking belongs to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said routine tasks go first. What would be left of the job you trained for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose what's left is judgement and talking to clients, the bits where someone has to sign their name and take blame. But those jobs go to people who already have five years behind them, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told me you never use AI tools. What would it take for you to change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if a union rep or my old tutor showed me, in person, one boring task done with AI that saved a real hour. Not a video, a person next to me. I'm slow with new tools and I know it.

say: I'd say **governments and unions** must set rules when firms replace graduate hiring with software.
I'd tell friends this is **not the workers' fault** and shouldn't be our bill.
think: The thinking tasks on the card are **exactly my entry-level work**, so I'm in the firing line.
I know I'm **slow with new tools**, and that scares me more than the machines.
do: Apply to **council and health service** finance teams, where unions and rulebooks still exist.
Join the **graduate union branch** and ask my mum's hospital friend about finance openings.
Take **one free course** on how software handles audits.
feel: I feel **angry and unfairly squeezed**, because the checking I trained for now belongs to a machine.
S1.quote: I studied for three years to be the person who checks things, and now the checking belongs to a machine.
fieldNote: Priya's anger points at **employers and policy**, never at the tools themselves.
She turns to **collective routes** first: union branch, public employers, rules.
She admits she is slow with technology, which makes her expect to lose out.

steps.text: Apply to council and hospital finance teams
Join the graduate branch of a trade union
Take one free online course on software in audits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an emergency and the government can't leave it to the market. Two years is nothing, so we need a public job guarantee and training money, and the companies that profit should pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I think my degree loses its worth almost overnight, and I'd have barely started my career before the whole desk-job route closes, and I don't even have a Plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first count every pound: loans, savings, my mum's night shifts. Then I'd ask my family whether I can stay home for years if needed. I'd apply for anything with hands-on elements, like care work or the garden centre, since robots arrive later, and I'd write to my local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a platform when the lights go out. I can't sleep properly just thinking about my little brother's university, because there might be no jobs to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what do you do differently in the first month than in the slow picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first big layoffs, I'd go to my mum and my aunt Samira, and honestly to the union and the councillor. I'd want to be around people marching, not sitting alone on a laptop at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you turn to, if anyone, when the first big layoffs hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd stop pretending it's a normal job hunt. I'd look at training for something hands-on, maybe a healthcare assistant course, because those jobs wait about three extra years for robots. That's a change from just sending ten applications a week.

say: I'd say the government can't leave this to the **market** and the companies profiting must pay.
I'd push for a **public job guarantee** and paid training for graduates.
think: My degree could **lose its worth overnight**, and I have no Plan B at all.
I fear my brother's **university plans** collapse because nobody will pay for them.
do: Count **every pound** of loans and savings and ask family about staying home long term.
Apply for **hands-on work** like care jobs, since robots arrive about three years later.
Write to my **local councillor** and join any march or union meeting I can find.
feel: I feel like I'm **standing in the dark**, awake at night, with a brother depending on a future I can't see.
S2.quote: I think my degree loses its worth almost overnight, and I'd have barely started my career before the whole desk-job route closes
fieldNote: Priya expects to **lose the whole route** into her profession, so alarmed is honest even with family help.
Her instinct is to go **towards people**: family, union, councillor.
The first-month plan shows a real shift: from applying to desk jobs to hands-on training.

steps.text: Write down every loan, saving and family help figure
Apply for healthcare assistant and care jobs
Write to my local councillor about a graduate job guarantee
Ask my mum and aunt if I can stay home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a bit less panicked in public. I'd say five years is enough for governments to act if they stop dithering, and I'd keep pushing for rules on using AI in hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be anxious, but there's room to maneuver. Maybe I get a first job in the council finance office for three years and save hard, then move into something that needs a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally get a proper first job, even a boring one, and save a third of my pay. I'd move out slowly, share a flat with a friend from uni, and keep up with my union branch. I'd also try an AI tool once, in the library, with someone beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a countdown clock, but at least I can see it. I feel less sick than with the two-year one, more like carrying a heavy bag than being pushed off a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you a bit of runway. What do you do with the first year of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother to study something he can't do from a screen alone, nursing or engineering or teaching. And to talk to people, because the person with the good references still gets hired when software does the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger brother about his studies in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year I'd just get any contract with a pension and learn the basics of how that office works. Even if AI changes it, I'd be inside, with colleagues who'd rather keep a known person than start again.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** for governments to act if they stop dithering.
I'd keep pushing for rules on **AI in hiring** with my union branch.
think: I'm still anxious, but there is **room to manoeuvre** if I get a first job soon.
A boring council job with a **pension** feels like the safest base.
do: Take any **first finance contract** and save about a third of every pay cheque.
Share a flat with a **uni friend** after six months and keep paying down loans.
Try an **AI tool once** in the library with someone sitting beside me.
feel: I feel a **countdown clock** ticking, but it's more like a heavy bag than a push off a bridge.
S3.quote: I'd tell my brother to study something he can't do from a screen alone, nursing or engineering or teaching.
fieldNote: Priya's tone is **calmer in public** than in private; the mood stays high because she still has no job.
More time lets her plan **inside a job** rather than flee the profession.
She now says she'd try an AI tool once, a small but real step.

steps.text: Take the first finance contract with a pension
Save a third of every pay cheque
Try one AI tool in the library with help
Keep attending my union branch meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people will cope, but only if firms are told to hire and train young people along the way. I'd say it's not a reason to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel fairly okay. Ten years is long enough for me to get a job, pay my loans and move out. I'd just be worried about the second half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, take whatever first role comes, and at the same time do a slow part-time course in something less exposed, maybe tax advice for families, where a human still sits across the table. I'd save for a deposit and not stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, a bit like a long winter. I'd still be tense on bad weeks, but I'm not lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still choose a desk career, or would you steer differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably keep an accounting career for the first five years, then slide into advice work or training new people. I'd want my loans gone by then, so I could take a pay cut if I have to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good version of those ten years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good version is a steady job by next spring, loans down to half, and my mum finally working days instead of nights. If that happens, AGI in 2036 is a problem for later me.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for people to cope, but only if firms keep **training** the young the young.
I'd say it is **no reason to relax**, even if it sounds far off.
think: Ten years is enough for me to get a job and **clear loans**, so I feel fairly okay.
I worry more about the **second half** of that decade than the first.
do: Take **whatever first role** comes and keep applying while I wait.
Start a slow **part-time course** in tax advice for families, where a person still sits across the table.
**Save for a deposit** and aim to clear half my loans in five years.
feel: It feels **manageable**, like a long winter, with tense bad weeks but no sleepless nights.
S4.quote: A good version is a steady job by next spring, loans down to half, and my mum finally working days instead of nights.
fieldNote: Priya's mood drops a level because she has **time to prepare**, but the jobless start keeps it from calm.
Her plan is about **people-facing work** like tax advice for families.
Her mum's night shifts remain the emotional anchor of her goals.

steps.text: Take the first accounting role offered
Start a part-time tax advice course
Save towards a house deposit and half the loans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd have no time to get even a first job before the whole desk route changed. What would help is a real public jobs plan, training that's paid for, and rules so companies can't just stop hiring graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't lazy. Sixty applications is a full-time job on its own, and nobody talks about how lonely it is. I'd like the people deciding all this to spend a morning at my kitchen table.

headlineQuote: Sixty applications is a full-time job on its own, and nobody talks about how lonely it is.
portrait: Priya is a 23-year-old **accounting graduate** in Hadley with no offer yet, living in the box room at her parents' flat.
She has about 14,000 in loans and **six weeks of savings**, with her night-shift nurse mum as the emotional anchor.
She leans left, blames employers and wants **unions** and public help, and she never uses AI tools.
Her mood climbs from anxious to alarmed, and her plans shift towards **hands-on and public-sector** work when time is short.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because she'd have no time to land a first job before desk work changes.
whatWouldHelp: A **public jobs plan**, paid training and rules stopping firms from dropping graduate hiring would help her most.
